turns.question: Our sonde spits out a number in uS/cm for salt. I get the microsiemens part, but what is the 'per centimetre' actually doing there - is that a reading divided by something, or a property of the water itself?
turns.answer:
The "per centimetre" reflects that conductivity is a property of the water itself, not just a raw reading. Electrical conductivity is "a measure of the electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit length and cross-sectional area" 【14†"a measure of the electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit length and cross-sectional area"】.

In practice, the meter measures a conductance (in siemens) between two electrode plates, and converts it using the cell constant — the ratio of the plate spacing to the plate area, in units of cm⁻¹ — via the equation κ = K_cell × G 【14†"where 𝐾cell is the cell constant (in units of cm-1)"】. So the geometry of the probe is divided out, leaving a value that describes the water's intrinsic ability to carry current, regardless of the particular probe's dimensions.

One related note: the USGS reports this as "specific conductance," which is the value corrected to what it would be at 25 °C, since conductivity changes with temperature 【14†"the value is corrected to what it would be at 25 °C and reported as specific conductance at 25 °C"】.

1.1 Overview of Specific Conductance
Specific conductance is an indirect measure of the collec-
tive concentration of dissolved ions in solution, and is defined
as the electrical conductance of 1 cubic centimeter (cm³) of a
solution at 25 degrees Celsius (°C) (Hem, 1982). The terms
“specific conductance,” “specific electrical conductance,” and
“electrical conductivity” have been used interchangeably in
the literature to report the same measurement. Because the
term “electrical conductivity” is not always referenced to a
standard temperature, the measurement or reference tempera-
ture must be reported with this parameter. The USGS National
Water Information System (NWIS) reports the measurement
of electrical conductance as specific conductance at 25 °C,
meaning that at any temperature for which the measurement
is made, the value is corrected to what it would be at 25 ºC.
The term “specific conductance” is correctly defined as the
electrical conductance of 1 cm³ of a solution at 25 °C. If the
electrical conductance is measured at another temperature, the
value is corrected to what it would be at 25 °C and reported as
specific conductance at 25 °C. Most modern specific con-
ductance meters are temperature compensated and report the
corrected value automatically.

Maintenance of specific conductance equipment includes
periodic inspections of meters and probes and checks on
instrument operation and performance.

regular cleaning is required.
2.2.1 Conductivity Probe Cleaning, Storage, and
Maintenance
Accurate and precise measurement of specific conduc-
tance requires a well-maintained and clean conductivity probe.
A probe that is dirty or wet with solution other than the sample
may contaminate the measured solution and bias the mea-
surement of specific conductance. Conductivity probes must
be clean and the electrodes free from scratches to produce
accurate results. Refer to the manufacturer’s instructions for
storage and additional maintenance information.
• To clean conductivity probes—
• Clean the probe thoroughly by rinsing with copious
amounts of deionized water (DIW) before and after
making a measurement. This is sufficient cleaning in
most cases.
• Epoxy and graphite conductivity probes can be
gently wiped with a clean laboratory tissue to
remove any residues.

The "per centimetre" reflects that conductivity is a property of the water itself, not just a raw reading. Electrical conductivity is "a measure of the electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit length and cross-sectional area" 【14†"a measure of the electrical conductance (G) of a substance normalized to a unit length and cross-sectional area"】.

In practice, the meter measures a conductance (in siemens) between two electrode plates, and converts it using the cell constant — the ratio of the plate spacing to the plate area, in units of cm⁻¹ — via the equation κ = K_cell × G 【14†"where 𝐾cell is the cell constant (in units of cm-1)"】. So the geometry of the probe is divided out, leaving a value that describes the water's intrinsic ability to carry current, regardless of the particular probe's dimensions.

One related note: the USGS reports this as "specific conductance," which is the value corrected to what it would be at 25 °C, since conductivity changes with temperature 【14†"the value is corrected to what it would be at 25 °C and reported as specific conductance at 25 °C"】.

turns.question: Someone dug up a survey of the same creek from decades back and every salt number in it is written in micromhos per centimetre. Do we have to convert those before we can put them next to ours?
turns.answer:
No conversion needed. The units are equivalent: "The units of electrical conductivity are siemens per centimeter (S/cm), which is the equivalent of mhos per centimeter (mhos/cm)" 【3†"The units of electrical conductivity are siemens per centimeter (S/cm), which is the equivalent of mhos per centimeter (mhos/cm)"】. So micromhos per centimetre and microsiemens per centimetre (μS/cm) are the same unit under an older name, and the old survey values can sit directly beside yours.

One thing worth checking before comparing: whether the old values were temperature-corrected to 25 °C, since conductivity changes with temperature and the reference temperature should be reported with the measurement 【3†"the measurement or reference temperature must be reported with this parameter"】.

1.1 Overview of Specific Conductance
Specific conductance is an indirect measure of the collec-
tive concentration of dissolved ions in solution, and is defined
as the electrical conductance of 1 cubic centimeter (cm³) of a
solution at 25 degrees Celsius (°C) (Hem, 1982). The terms
“specific conductance,” “specific electrical conductance,” and
“electrical conductivity” have been used interchangeably in
the literature to report the same measurement. Because the
term “electrical conductivity” is not always referenced to a
standard temperature, the measurement or reference tempera-
ture must be reported with this parameter. The USGS National
Water Information System (NWIS) reports the measurement
of electrical conductance as specific conductance at 25 °C,
meaning that at any temperature for which the measurement
is made, the value is corrected to what it would be at 25 ºC.
The term “specific conductance” is correctly defined as the
electrical conductance of 1 cm³ of a solution at 25 °C. If the
electrical conductance is measured at another temperature, the
value is corrected to what it would be at 25 °C and reported as
specific conductance at 25 °C. Most modern specific con-
ductance meters are temperature compensated and report the
corrected value automatically.

4.3 Measurement of Specific Conductance of a
Water Sample with Low or High pH
Specific conductance (and electrical conductivity) data
are reported at 25 °C. Most modern specific conductance
meters have the capability to compensate for temperature auto-
matically. Equation 2 is used most commonly to determine the
specific conductance at 25 °C and commercially available field
specific conductance meters typically use either a constant α
(typically 0.019–0.020 per °C) or a nonlinear α (International
Organization for Standardization, 1985). Whereas these com-
monly used temperature-compensation factors work well for
waters having a pH between 4 and 11, they can be the source
of errors as large as 50 percent for low-pH samples.
4.3.1 Measurement of Specific Conductance of
a Water Sample with Low pH (<4)
The specific conductance measurement error for low-pH
(<4) waters can be large if the commonly used temperature-
compensation factors are used. To determine whether an alter-
native temperature-compensation method should be used for
samples with pH <4, the in situ specific conductance should
be compared to the specific conductance of a sample equili-
brated to 25 °C. If the measurements are comparable (within
±5 μS/cm for specific conductance ≤100 μS/cm or ±3 percent
for specific conductance >100 μS/cm), then the temperature
algorithm used is likely sufficient. If a temperature-compen-
sation factor is required for a water sample with pH <4, the
method described by McCleskey (2013) is recommended.
4.3.2 Measurement of Specific Conductance of
a Water Sample with High pH (>11)
No temperature-compensation method is available for
waters with high pH (>11); therefore, the specific conduc-
tance should be checked by making a measurement at ambient
temperature and at 25 °C for waters with pH >11. At high pH,
hydroxide becomes a major ion in the solution and its mobility
is different than that of most other ions. However, the hydrox-
ide-equivalent conductivity is much lower than the hydrogen-
equivalent conductivity and, unlike in low-pH waters, the stan-
dard temperature-compensation approaches may be adequate.
Furthermore, relatively few natural waters have a pH >11, so
this situation is fairly rare.
